ety.text: From Middle English viage, borrowed from Anglo-Norman viage and Old French voiage, from Latin viaticum. The modern spelling is under the influence of Modern French voyage. Doublet of viaticum.

senses.d: A long journey, especially by ship.
ex: He went on a voyage to France.
I love a Sea voyage and a bluſtring tempeſt; [...]

senses.d: A written account of a journey or travel.
ex: By the various Relations, Embaſſies and Voyages of Siam that have been publiſht within theſe laſt Four Years […]

senses.d: The act or practice of travelling.
ex: [...] [A]ll Nations haue Enterknowledge one of another, either by Voyage into Forreine Parts, or by Strangers that come to them: [...]

senses.d: To go on a long journey.
ex: A mind forever voyaging through strange seas of thought alone.
O soul, voyagest thou indeed on voyages like those? / Disportest thou on waters such as those?
